transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… so the biggest reason I finally made the appointment is that at work I keep getting up from my workstation during the day, even when I know I’m supposed to just stay there and finish reviewing claims.

I’m a claims processing clerk, so a lot of my job is sitting there going through files and policy stuff, and I’ll tell myself, like, “Okay, just finish this batch,” but then I’m up again — getting water, walking around, checking something that probably didn’t need checking right then. It’s not like I don’t understand I’m supposed to stay put. I do. That’s actually what’s frustrating, because I’ll be aware that I need to sit and finish the review, and somehow I still end up leaving my desk. It’s started to feel like it’s getting in the way enough that I should talk to someone about it.
Can you tell me what goes through your mind when you get up from your desk? Are you feeling like you have to check something specific or do you just feel restless and need to move?

It’s usually not like there’s one specific important thing I have to check. Sometimes I’ll kind of tell myself there is, like, “Oh, I should go refill my water,” or “I’ll just walk over and see if that file is there,” but honestly a lot of the time it feels more like I just… get pulled out of staying at the desk.

I’ll know I’m supposed to sit there and keep working through the claim reviews, and I’ll even be aware that getting up is going to interrupt me, but then I still do it. It’s like the thought is very immediate — “I need to get up for a second” — and then I’m already away from the workstation. And then afterward I’ll think, “Why did I do that? I was supposed to finish that batch.”

So I guess it’s less about checking one particular thing and more that I have a hard time staying put at the workstation, even when I know that’s exactly what I’m supposed to be doing.
Outside of work, do you find yourself acting on sudden impulses — like saying something without thinking it through, making quick decisions you later regret, or starting tasks and not finishing them?

Um… outside of work, I’m honestly not sure how much that happens. I mean, I can think of normal stuff, like deciding to start something around the apartment and then getting sidetracked, but I don’t know if I’d call it sudden impulses in the way you mean.

Like, I don’t really have a clear example of blurting something out and regretting it, or making some big quick decision that caused problems. At least nothing is jumping out at me. The work thing is just much more obvious because I’m supposed to be at the desk doing one thing, so when I get up it’s very noticeable.

Outside work it’s a little harder for me to tell what’s just normal distracted behavior versus something I should be paying attention to.
Looking back, did you have similar issues with staying focused or acting on impulse when you were a child, like in school or at home?

Yeah… looking back, I don’t think this is totally new. I didn’t really think of it that way at the time, because when you’re a kid you just kind of assume school is hard in whatever way it’s hard for you, but I do remember getting comments from teachers in elementary school.

It was usually something like, “He’s bright,” or “He understands the material,” but then there’d be the other part — that I lost worksheets, or I missed instructions, or I needed reminders to actually finish the classwork. Like I could know what we were doing, but somehow I’d misplace the paper or not catch the next step because I wasn’t fully tuned in when they explained it. And then the teacher would have to come over and be like, “Okay, you need to keep going,” or remind me what I was supposed to be doing.

So, yeah, I guess there was a pattern even back then. It wasn’t like I was failing everything or didn’t understand it, which maybe made it easier to overlook, but the comments were definitely there — bright, but not staying on top of the actual work and instructions.
In your current life outside of work and school, do you find it hard to focus, stay organized, or control the urge to act quickly without thinking?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because outside of work and school there isn’t always, like, one clear standard I’m being measured against, if that makes sense.

At home, I can have times where I mean to do something and then I kind of drift into something else, but I don’t know how much of that is just normal. Like if I’m not on a clock or no one’s waiting for me to finish a specific assignment, it’s harder for me to tell whether I’m genuinely having trouble focusing or just being kind of unstructured.

With organization, I wouldn’t say I have some obvious system that’s great, but I also don’t know if I can point to a major pattern outside of work. And with acting quickly without thinking, I don’t really have a strong example that comes to mind. I’m not someone who’s constantly making big impulsive choices, at least not that I’ve noticed.

So I guess my honest answer is: maybe a little with focus or keeping myself on track when there’s no structure, but I’m not really sure. It’s much more obvious to me in settings where there’s a task I’m supposed to stay with.

When you're at home or in situations without a strict schedule or task, do you find it hard to start or finish things you mean to do, or do you often feel pulled toward doing something else before finishing what you started?

Yeah, I think… the closest thing I can describe is that my attention gets pulled off pretty easily, even when I’m trying to stay with something. Like at home, if I’m reading through something or trying to deal with some paperwork or even just focusing on a specific thing on my phone, and then I hear people nearby talking about something else — especially if it’s something that reminds me of another claim or some random errand I forgot — my brain just sort of jumps over there.

It’s not always like I consciously decide, “Oh, I’m going to stop doing this now.” It’s more like I’ll realize I haven’t actually absorbed the last paragraph or whatever I was looking at. Then I have to go back and reread the same section a few times, which is frustrating because I technically had my eyes on it, but I wasn’t really taking it in.

So, yeah, I guess in situations without a strict schedule, it’s less that I’m making some big impulsive choice to abandon things, and more that something nearby catches my attention or I remember some unrelated errand, and suddenly I’m not really with the thing I was doing anymore.
Do you often feel physically restless or find yourself fidgeting, tapping your hands or feet, or moving around when you're expected to stay still, like in meetings or while sitting for long periods?

Yeah, I do notice that, especially in situations where I’m supposed to just sit and listen for a while.

Like in trainings at work, or longer team meetings, I’m usually doing something with my body even if I’m trying not to be obvious about it. I’ll be bouncing my leg under the table, or clicking my pen, or shifting around in the chair a lot. Sometimes I’ll catch myself doing it and stop, and then a minute later I’m doing it again without really deciding to.

It’s not like I feel like I have to get up and run around or anything dramatic, but staying completely still for a long stretch feels kind of uncomfortable. I’m usually trying to look focused and professional, so I’ll keep it small — like moving my foot, changing positions, messing with a pen — but yeah, it’s definitely there in meetings or trainings that go on for a while.

Can you describe any situations — either recently or in the past — where you found it really hard to pay attention, or where you felt overly active or unable to stay still, even when it was important to do so?

Yeah, the clearest example — and honestly kind of the main reason I finally decided I should come in and talk to someone — is at work with my workstation.

I’m a claims processing clerk, so a lot of my day is sitting there reviewing claims or policy information, and I know I’m supposed to stay at my desk and just work through them. It’s not like I don’t understand that. But I keep getting up during the day, even when I know I really need to stay put and finish the claim reviews. Like I’ll be sitting there trying to get through a batch, and then I’ll just feel like I need to stand up or walk away for a minute. Sometimes it’s to get water, or check something, or just… I don’t even know, just not be sitting there anymore.

And then afterward I’m frustrated with myself because it’s not like I was done. The claim is still sitting there waiting, and I’m aware that I’ve interrupted myself again. It feels especially stupid because the task is important, and I do know that I’m expected to stay focused and keep moving through them. But in the moment, staying in that seat and continuing feels harder than it seems like it should.

That’s the example that stands out the most to me — not some dramatic situation, but just repeatedly leaving my workstation when I’m supposed to be finishing the work in front of me.
